rows.speaker: غير واحد
rows.claim: The conventional question “who is more unjust?” denies that anyone equals or surpasses the named wrongdoer, although the syntax alone does not state that denial.
rows.anchor: وقد قال غير واحد إن قولك : من أظلم ممن فعل كذا إنكار لأن يكون أحد أظلم منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers the earlier answers with their relevant qualification, or a hyperbolic threat that makes no factual claim about comparative rank; either removes the objection.
rows.anchor: فلعل الأولى الرجوع إلى أحد الجوابين مع ملاحظة الحيثية وإن جعلت ذلك الكلام مخرجا مخرج المبالغة في التهديد والزجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may be the second object of “prevent,” a causal phrase, or an explicative genitive construction with an omitted second object; alternatively, people are the object and the verb takes one object.
rows.anchor: أن يذكر فيها أسمه مفعول ثان لمنع أو مفعول من أجله بمعنى منعها كراهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning God's name stands for the prayers and devotional acts, inward and outward, that are permitted in mosques.
rows.anchor: وكنى بذكر أسم الله تعالى عما يوقع في المساجد من الصلوات والتقربات إلى الله تعالى بالأفعال القلبية والقالبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking to ruin the mosques means demolishing them and disabling their use.
rows.anchor: وسعى في خرابها أي هدمها وتعطيلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those” refers to the wrongdoers who prevent worship and seek to ruin the mosques.
rows.anchor: أولئك الظالمون المانعون الساعون في خرابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one reading, the lām expresses fitting entitlement and fear means awe of God; the clause answers what conduct would suit them and treats injustice as putting things out of place.
rows.anchor: اللامفي ( لهم ) إما للاختصاص على وجه اللياقة كما في الحل للفرس والمراد من الخوف الخوف من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the lām expresses deserved entitlement and fear means fear of believers; this answers what right the mosque-destroyers had and frames injustice as violating another's right.
rows.anchor: وإما للاستحقاق كما فيالجنة للمؤمن والمراد من الخوفالخوف من المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the clause states what God decreed would happen in the future: the disbelievers would enter only fearfully. It is a parenthetical promise to aid believers and free the mosques from them.
rows.anchor: في علم الله تعالى وقضائه ( أن يدخلوها ) فيما سيجيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed report says that Christians entered Jerusalem's sanctuary only in disguise and stealthily.
rows.anchor: فقد روى أنه لا يدخل بيت المقدس أحد من النصارى إلا متنكرا مسارقة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says any Christian found in Jerusalem was beaten and severely punished.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : لا يوجد نصراني في بيت المقدس إلا انتهك ضربا وأبلغ إليه في العقوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Crusader capture of Jerusalem for over a century before Saladin retook it does not refute the promise: it need only have been fulfilled at some point, not repeatedly.
rows.anchor: ولا نقض بإستيلاء الأقرع وبقاء بيت المقدس في أيدي النصارى أكثر من مائة سنة إلى أن أستخلصه الملك صلاح الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read the negation as a prohibition against enabling their entry, which entails fearful entry; Al-Alusi prefers from the outset the direct reading as a promise of believers' victory and recovery of the mosques.
rows.anchor: وقيل : النفي بمعنى النهي ومعناه على طريق الكناية النهي عن التخلية والتمكين من دخولهم

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa allows non-Muslims to enter mosques generally, citing this verse, the Prophet's lodging the Thaqif delegation in the mosque, and the sanctuary-safety report; he reads the prohibition as disapproval or as limited to entering the Haram for pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: فجوزه الإمام أبو حنيفة رضي الله تعالى عنه مطلقا للآية فإنها تفيد دخولهم بخشية وخشوع

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik bars non-Muslims from mosques, citing 9:28 and the duty to purify mosques from impurity, though the passage also reports permission for need.
rows.anchor: ومنعه مالك رضي الله تعالى عنه مطلقا لقوله تعالى : ( إنما المشركون نجس ) والمساجد يجب تطهيرها

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i distinguishes the Sacred Mosque from other mosques and regards the cited hadith as abrogated by the verse.
rows.anchor: فرق الإمام الشافعي رضي الله تعالى عنه بين المسجد الحرام وغيره

rows.speaker: عبدالله
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allah gives “إلا حنيفا.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبدالله ( إلا حنيفا ) وهو مثل صيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their worldly disgrace includes killing their leaders and chiefs, breaking idols, exposing their folly, and expelling them from Arabia, or imposing the jizya on those made protected subjects.
rows.anchor: خزي أي عظيم بقتل أبطالهم وأقيالهم وكسر أصنامهم وتسفيه أحلامهم وإخراجهم من جزيرة العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The great punishment of the hereafter is Hell, matching the great scale of their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: ولهم في الآخرة عذاب عظيم وهو عذاب النار لما أن سببه أيضا وهو ما حكى من ظلمهم كذلك في العظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting the locative phrases first in both clauses builds anticipation for the punishment that follows.
rows.anchor: وتقديم الظرف في الموضعين للتشويق لما يذكر بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the inward reading, God's mosques are hearts where He is known and worshipped through self-annihilation.
rows.anchor: مواضع السجود لله تعالى وهي القلوب التي يعرف فيها فيسجد له بالفناء الذاتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine name may mean the Supreme Name, whose theophany occurs in the heart as the manifestation of the Essence with all attributes, or each person's name suited to their capacity.
rows.anchor: الاسم الأعظم إذ لا يتجلى بهذا الاسم إلا في القلب وهو التجلي بالذات مع جميع الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inward ruin is clouding hearts with fanaticism and passion, and stirring conflicts among the soul's powers, satanic impulse, and illusion.
rows.anchor: بتكديرها بالتعصبات وغلبة الهوى ومنع أهلها بتهييج الفتن اللازمة لتجاذب قوى النفس وداعي الشيطان والوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They can approach these hearts only fearful and humbled before the manifestation of the Real.
rows.anchor: منكسرين لظهور تجلي الحق فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the inward reading, worldly disgrace exposes their falsehood and the afterlife punishment is veiling from God.
rows.anchor: وافتضاح وذلة بظهور بطلان ما هم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet repeatedly turned his gaze toward the sky, eagerly expecting revelation about the direction of prayer.
rows.anchor: أي كثيرا ما نرى تردد وجهك وتصرف نظرك في جهة السماء متشوفا للوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He hoped God would turn him toward the Kaaba because Jews taunted him for following their qibla, and because it was Abraham's and the older qibla, more likely to draw Arabs to faith.
rows.anchor: يتوقع من ربه أن يحوله إلى الكعبة لما أن اليهود كانوا يقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi thinks the Prophet awaited the change without explicitly asking; the verse's failure to mention a request suggests this and reflects his perfect propriety.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم لم يسأل ذلك من ربه بل كان ينتظر فقط إذ لو وقع السؤال لكان الظاهر ذكره

rows.speaker: قتادة والسدي وغيرهما
rows.claim: Qatada, al-Suddi, and others say the Prophet repeatedly prayed to God to change the qibla to the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة والسدي وغيرهما : كان رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يقلب وجهه في الدعاء إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that account, the Prophet's request may have followed permission, since prophets do not ask without authorization lest an ungranted request become a trial for their people.
rows.anchor: لعل ذلك بعد حصول الإذن له بالدعاء لما أن الأنبياء لا يسألون الله تعالى شيئا من غير أن يؤذن لهم فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed report says the Prophet asked Gabriel for permission to pray, and Gabriel told him God had permitted it.
rows.anchor: أخبره بأن الله تعالى قد أذن له بالدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects the need for explicit permission: the Prophet could ask for a religious benefit he understood, given his exceptional nearness to God; any admonition addressed hidden wisdom, not a lapse in his manners.
rows.anchor: والذي أراه أنه لا مانع من دعائه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم وسؤاله التحويل لمصلحة ألهمها ومنفعة دينية فهمها ولا يتوقف ذلك على الاستئذان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite allowing that he could have asked, Al-Alusi thinks he did not explicitly pray in this incident: sound reports show only his desire for the change.
rows.anchor: حيث لم يكن فيها سوى حب التحويل

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: Al-Bara reports that the Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem for sixteen months after reaching Medina, then God revealed the verse, knowing the Prophet's desire.
rows.anchor: قال : صلينا مع رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بعد قدومه المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take “قد” here to indicate rarity, arguing that infrequent glances better show the Prophet's perfect manners.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من جعل ( قد ) هنا للتقليل زعما منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi objects that one upward glance is not called repeated turning; the word therefore conveys frequent turning in this context.
rows.anchor: مرة واحدة لا يقال له : قلب بصره إلى السماء وإنما يقال : قلب إذا داوم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: The frequency may be a lexical force of “قد” or an inference from the actual context; the latter account is attributed to Sibawayh.
rows.anchor: قولان نسب ثانيهما إلى سيبويه

rows.speaker: بعض النحاة
rows.claim: Some grammarians say “قد” shifts a present verb into the past, citing 24:64 and 15:97 as parallels.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعض النحاة أن ( قد ) تقلب المضارع ماضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We will turn you toward a qibla” means either granting him the ability to face it or making him face its direction.
rows.anchor: من قولك : وليته كذا إذا جعلته واليا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ marks the result of what precedes and introduces an implicit oath, whose lām intensifies the certainty of the promise.
rows.anchor: والفاء لسببية ما قبلها لما بعدها وهي في الحقيقة داخلة على قسم محذوف تدل عليه اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise comes before the command so the Prophet rejoices first at the answer and again when it is fulfilled.
rows.anchor: وجاء قبل الأمر لفرح انفس بالإجابة ثم بإنجاز الوعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this construction, the verb takes two objects: the addressed person is first and the qibla is second.
rows.anchor: ونولي يتعدى لإثنين الكاف الأول وقبلة الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You are pleased with” means that he loves and inclines toward it for sound purposes consonant with God's will and wisdom.
rows.anchor: أي تحبها وتميل إليها للأغراض الصحيحة التي أضمرتها ووافقت مشيئة الله تعالى وحكمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You are pleased with” is an accusative adjective of “qibla”; the noun is indefinite because no particular qibla has yet been mentioned, and the wording does not specify one already requested.
rows.anchor: نصب صفة لقبلة ونكرها لأنه لم يجر قبلها ما يقتضي أن تكون معهودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command branches from the promise; the face is specified because it is the axis and measure of orientation, though it may stand metonymically for the whole body as the noblest and distinguishing limb.
rows.anchor: الفاء لتفريع الأمر على الوعد وتخصيص التولية بالوجه لما أنه مدار التوجه ومعياره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains “shatr” as toward the Sacred Mosque.
rows.anchor: أي نحوه كما روى عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali explains “shatr” as in its direction or facing it.
rows.anchor: أو قبله كما روى عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains “shatr” as toward it or in its direction.
rows.anchor: أو تلقاءه كما روى عن قتادة ظرف مكان مبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the verb has one object, “your face,” and “shatr” is an ambiguous locative adverb equivalent to “toward,” with an omitted “to”; this yields direct alignment with the qibla.
rows.anchor: ظرف مكان مبهم كمفسره منصوب على الظرفية أغنى غناء إلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects making “shatr” a second object: that would mean making oneself face the mosque's direction, rather than turning the face toward the qibla as fulfillment of the promise requires.
rows.anchor: لأن ترتبه بالفاء وكونه إنجازا للوعد بأن الله تعالى يجعل مستقبل القبلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative takes “shatr” originally as a separated portion, then a side or part, making it a second object; Al-Alusi says this remains ill-suited to the promised turning, and “half” is untenable.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الشطر في الأصل لما أنفصل عن الشيء ثم أستعمل لجانبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Al-Haram” means either a place where fighting is forbidden or a place protected from aggressors.
rows.anchor: والحرام المحرم أي محرم فيه القتال أو ممنوع من الظلمة أن يتعرضوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming the Sacred Mosque rather than the Kaaba shows that a distant worshipper need only align with the qibla's direction, not hit the Kaaba's exact point.
rows.anchor: مع أنها القبلة التي دلت عليها الأحاديث الصحاح إشارة إلى أنه يكفي للبعيد محاذاة جهة القبلة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأحمد وأكثر الخراسانيين من الشافعية
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa, Ahmad, most Khurasani Shafi'is, and al-Ghazali in the Ihya hold that a distant worshipper faces the direction of the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: مذهب أبي حنيفة رضي الله تعالى عنه وأحمد وقول أكثر الخراسانيين من الشافعية

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأحمد وأكثر الخراسانيين من الشافعية
rows.claim: Even those who require facing the Kaaba's direction say the worshipper must intend the Kaaba itself as the qibla.
rows.anchor: إلا إنهم قالوا : يجب أن يكون قصد المتوجه إلى الجهة

rows.speaker: العراقيون والقفال
rows.claim: The Iraqi Shafi'is and al-Qaffal require facing the Kaaba's exact point.
rows.anchor: وقال العراقيون والقفال منهم : يجب إصابة العين

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says the Kaaba is the qibla for people in the mosque, the mosque for Makkans, the Haram for Makkah, and Makkah's sanctuary for the world.
rows.anchor: مسجد قبلة مكة وهي قبلة الحرم وهو قبلة الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A Prophetic report from Ibn Abbas supports the tiered qibla view; the disagreement concerns those not physically present, since present worshippers must face the Kaaba exactly by consensus.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما مرفوعا ما يدل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse omits an explicit reference to prayer because the requested direction was the only matter at issue; another view says the verse came while the Prophet was praying, making that context sufficient.
rows.anchor: ولم يقيد سبحانه وتعالى التولية في الصلاة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi and others say the Prophet prayed toward Jerusalem for sixteen months, then in Rajab, two months before Badr, turned during Zuhr at Banu Salima; men and women exchanged rows and the mosque became the Mosque of the Two Qiblas.
rows.anchor: ذكره القاضي تبعا لغيره أنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti calls that account a distortion: the Banu Salima story did not have the Prophet leading or turning during prayer.
rows.anchor: كما قال الإمام السيوطيتحريف للحديث

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد بن المعلى
rows.claim: Al-Nasa'i reports from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla that he and a companion heard the verse while the Prophet sat on the minbar; they prayed two rak'ahs before he descended, then he led the people in Zuhr.
rows.anchor: أخرج النسائي عن أبي سعيد بن المعلى قال : كنا نغدو إلى المسجد

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Abu Dawud reports from Anas that while the Prophet and companions prayed toward Jerusalem, a caller at Banu Salima announced the change during Fajr; they turned toward the Kaaba while still bowing.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو داؤد عن أنس رضي الله تعالى عنه أن النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects relying on the account that makes the Prophet turn during prayer at Banu Salima because it conflicts with sound, established reports.
rows.anchor: فما ذكر مخالف للروايات الصحيحة الثابتة عند أهل هذا الشأن فلا يعول عليه

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy's reading, “تلقاء المسجد الحرام,” supports interpreting “shatr” as toward.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي ( تلقاء المسجد الحرام ) وهي تؤيد القول الأول في ( شطر )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause attaches to the first command, completing the promise; “wherever” with “ma” is conditional, and “kana” is complete, meaning wherever you are found.
rows.anchor: عطف على ( فول وجهك ) ومن تتمة إنجاز الوعد والفاء جواب الشرط

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra does not require “ma” for “haythu” to function conditionally.
rows.anchor: والفراء لا يشترط ذلك فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wallu” derives from “wallayu”: the heavy vowel on yāʾ is dropped, then the first of two meeting consonants is deleted, producing the form faʿū.
rows.anchor: وأصل ( ولوا ) وليوا فأستثقلت الضمة على الياء فحذفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This explicitly generalizes the qibla ruling: an address to the Prophet applies to everyone unless evidence restricts it to him.
rows.anchor: وهذا تصريح بعموم الحكم المستفاد من السابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for naming every place is to prevent people from thinking this qibla applied only to the people of Medina.
rows.anchor: أن هذه القبلة مختصة بأهل المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the change from the Kaaba to Jerusalem sought Jewish goodwill, so the verse stresses facing the Kaaba even where Jews are present.
rows.anchor: لا يتوجه إليها في حضورهم أشار إلى تعميم التولية جميع الأمكنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation is to clarify that the Kaaba's direction remains obligatory even when Jerusalem is present, lest its presence be thought to prevent that orientation.
rows.anchor: فرض مع حضور بيت المقدس ولأهله أيضا لئلا يظن

rows.speaker: عبدالله
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allah says, “turn your faces toward it.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبدالله ( فولوا وجوهكم قبله )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those given the Book” means the Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: وإن الذين أوتوا الكتاب ( أي من اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book know the change is true because Muhammad would not command falsehood, each law has its own qibla, and their books foretold that he would pray toward both qiblas.
rows.anchor: لا يأمر بالباطل إذ هو النبي المبشر به في كتبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and Abraham share the Kaaba as qibla because they share a religious law, as indicated by the call to follow Abraham's upright religion.
rows.anchor: على ما ينبيء عنه قوله تعالى : ( بل ملة إبراهيم حنيفا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause is linked to “We see” because the first states the change and this one establishes its truth; alternatively, it is parenthetical reinforcement of the qibla command.
rows.anchor: والجملة عطف على ( قد نرى ) بجامع أن السابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing clause is parenthetical, promising and warning the two groups from the People of the Book, those who conceal and those who do not.
rows.anchor: اعتراض بين الكلامين جيء به للوعد والوعيد للفريقين من أهل الكتاب الداخلين تحت العموم السابق المشار إليهما فيما سيجيء

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read “تعملون” in the second person; this promises the believers, while the third-person reading warns the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي ( تعملون ) بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the pronoun in either reading to include all people, making the clause a promise and threat for believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الضمير على القراءتين لجميع الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description signals that reward belongs to those who remain patient when the affliction first strikes, as the report says patience is at the first shock.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أن الأجر لمن صبر وقت إصابتها كما في الخبر إنما الصبر عند أول صدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A misfortune includes every unpleasant harm to a person, property, or family, great or small—even a thorn, mosquito bite, broken sandal strap, or extinguished lamp.
rows.anchor: والمصيبة تعم ما يصيب الإنسان من مكروه في نفس أو مال

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet sought God's protection and reward after even minor harms, and said that anything painful to a believer is a misfortune bringing reward.
rows.anchor: استرجع النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم من ذلك وقال : كل ما يؤذي المؤمن

words: قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience is not merely verbal istirja: the heart also recalls its purpose of knowing God and perfecting the self, return to the Lord and eternal life, departure from this fleeting world, and God's greater blessings, then submits.
rows.anchor: وليس الصبر بالاسترجاع باللسان بل الصبر باللسان وبالقلب بأن يخطر بباله ما خلق لأجله من معرفة الله تعالى وتكميل نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience is distinctive to human beings because reason and desire contend within them.
rows.anchor: والصبر من خواص الإنسان لأنه يتعارض فيه العقل والشهوة

words: قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh report from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet said this community received a response to misfortune unavailable to other nations: “We belong to God, and to Him we return.”
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنه

words: قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report says earlier prophets did not receive this response; had Jacob received it, he would have said it when grieving for Joseph.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنه

words: قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: It is recommended after istirja to ask God to reward one in the affliction and replace it with something better; Muslim reports Umm Salama followed the Prophet's instruction after Abu Salama died and was given the Prophet as a better replacement.
rows.anchor: عن أم سلمة قالت : سمت رسول الله صلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “give glad tidings” is omitted; it means glad tidings of immense mercy and abundant beneficence.
rows.anchor: ومفعول ( بشر ) محذوف أي برحمة عظيمة وإحسان جزيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift to addressing the Prophet while speaking of “My servants” honors him and raises his rank.
rows.anchor: في تلوين الخطاب مع توجيهه لسيد ذوي الألباب عليه الصلاة والسلام ما لا يخفى من التشريف ورفع المحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question concerns God's nearness or distance, not His essence.
rows.anchor: عني أي عن قربي وبعدي إذ ليس السؤال عن ذاته تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted command to tell them is required for the conditional answer to follow; its omission shows God undertook the answer Himself rather than leaving it to the Messenger.
rows.anchor: أي فقل لهم ذلك بأن تخبر عن القرب بأي طريق كان ولا بد من التقدير إذ بدونه لا يترتب على الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's nearness is metaphorical, since spatial proximity is impossible for Him; it denotes His knowledge of servants' acts and words and awareness of their states.
rows.anchor: والقرب حقيقة في القرب المكاني المنزه عنه تعالى فهو استعارة لعلمه تعالى بأفعال العباد وأقوالهم وإطلاعه على سائر أحوالهم

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn Uyayna and Abdullah ibn Ahmad report from Ubayy that Muslims asked whether their Lord was near enough for private conversation or far enough to require calling aloud, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: عن أبي قال : قال المسلمون يارسول الله أقريب ربنا فنناجيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's answering the supplicant explains and confirms His nearness; the direct transition conveys intimacy, and “when” promises an answer in general rather than a guaranteed fulfillment of every request.
rows.anchor: دليل للقرب وتقرير له فالقطع لكمال الاتصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi sees no need to qualify the promise by God's will, redefine answering as merely “Here I am,” or restrict it to sinless requests or obedient supplicants, though piety helps.
rows.anchor: فلا حاجة إلى التقييد بالمشيئة المؤذن به قوله تعالى في آية أخرى : ( فيكشف ما تدعون إليه إن شاء )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A devout, humble supplicant is more likely to receive an answer, especially at particular times, places, and in recognized ways.
rows.anchor: نعم كونه كذلك أزجى للإجابة لا سيما في الأزمنة المخصوصة والأمكنة المعلومة والكيفية المشهورة

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: In a sound report from Abu Sa'id, the Prophet says a Muslim's lawful supplication brings one of three outcomes: immediate answer, deferred reward, or protection from equivalent harm.
rows.anchor: في الصحيح عن أبي سعيد قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Let them respond to Me” may mean ask Me to answer their prayers, or answer My call to faith and obedience as I answer their needs.
rows.anchor: أي فليطلبوا إجابتي لهم إذا دعوني أو فليجيبوا لي إذا دعوتهم للإيمان والطاعة كما أني أجيبهم إذا دعوني لحوائجهم

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators take the command to mean that people should answer God's call to faith and obedience; “believe in Me” then calls for steadfastness in faith.
rows.anchor: وهذا ما عليه أكثر المفسرين ولا يغني عنه وليؤمنوا بي لأنه أمر بالثبات والمداومة على الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to believe is not redundant with responding to God: it commands persistence and constancy in faith.
rows.anchor: ولا يغني عنه وليؤمنوا بي لأنه أمر بالثبات والمداومة على الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Perhaps they will be rightly guided” means guided to the interests of their religion and worldly life; the root sense is attaining good.
rows.anchor: أي يهتدون لمصالح دينهم ودنياهم وأصل الباب إصابة الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word is also read with the shin vowel opened or kasra-marked.
rows.anchor: وقريء بفتح الشين وكسرها ولما أمرهم سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the commands about fasting the month, counting its days, and magnifying and thanking God, this verse stresses that He knows deeds, hears words, and repays them; alternatively, amid abrogation it reassures believers of His knowledge, power, and kindness.
rows.anchor: ولما أمرهم سبحانه وتعالى بصوم الشهر ومراعاة العدة وحثهم على القيام بوظائف التكبير والشكر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and others explain “if they desist” as abandoning disbelief through repentance.
rows.anchor: عن الكفر بالتوبة منه كما روى عن مجاهد وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes their desisting to mean stopping both disbelief and fighting, as the surrounding mention of both suggests.
rows.anchor: أو عنه وعن القتال كما قيل : لقرينة ذكر الأمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they repent, God forgives their past wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: فيغفر لهم ما قد سلف

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Bahr cites this verse to support acceptance of repentance by a deliberate murderer: disbelief is graver than murder, yet repentance from disbelief is accepted.
rows.anchor: واستدل به في البحر على قبول توبة قاتل العمد إذ كان الكفر أعظم مأثما من القتل وقد أخبر سبحانه أنه يقبل التوبة منه
